newsitem.title: CANADA: MacMillan Bloedel posts big fourth quarter loss.
newsitem.headline: MacMillan Bloedel posts big fourth quarter loss.

text.p: MacMillan Bloedel Ltd. reported heavy fourth quarter losses on Tuesday, which analysts said would likely increase shareholder pressure for a major shake-up at Canada's biggest lumber and paper maker.
MacMillan Bloedel reported a loss of C$72 million ($53 million) in the fourth quarter ended Dec. 31, which included C$66 million ($49 million) in restructuring costs and asset writedowns.
In the same period last year when most of its markets were stronger, MacMillan had a C$68 million ($50 million) net profit.
Net earnings for 1996 plummeted to C$51 million ($37 million) from C$280 million ($206 million) in 1995.

"Although we expect to see some improvement in our markets during 1997, we need to further reduce costs to generate an acceptable return on assets," MacMillan Chief Executive Officer Bob Findlay said in a statement.
On a per share basis, the fourth-quarter loss was 60 cents Canadian (44 cents) per share compared with a profit of C50 cents (37 cents) a share.
The fourth-quarter loss was in the upper range of analysts' forecasts for a loss of between C42 cents (31 cents) and C69 cents (51 cents) per share.

MacMillan has been under intense pressure from shareholders, including big pension funds, disappointed by its performance. Speculation has swirled since last summer that the company would embark on a major restructuring that might include the departure of Findlay.
MacMillan's stock has been a sluggish performer in recent years despite strong paper prices in 1994 and 1995.
MacMillan closed down C15 cents (11 cents) at C$17.35 ($12.80) on the Toronto Stock Exchange, off its 52-week high of C$20.10 ($14.80).

The fourth-quarter charges included C$45 million ($33 million) in writedowns of old boilers being replaced at the Powell River paper mill in 1997, and MacMillan's investment in Oregon-based American Cemwood, which makes synthetic cedar shake roofing material.
The subsidiary dominated the market until the entry of Re-Con Building Products Inc. three years ago.
The remaining C$21 million ($15 million) was for costs related to streamlining the head office and business units.
Findlay said lower prices for pulp logs and chips, panelboards and packaging products together cut operating earnings by about C$280 million ($206 million).
Higher logging costs due to tougher harvesting regulations also reduced MacMillan's operating earnings.
In the Clayoquot Sound rain forest of Vancouver Island, timber harvests have fallen sharply since 1993 after fierce environmental protests forced tougher government regulations.
MacMillan's image also has suffered as environmental groups pushed for a European boycotts of its products.
MacMillan harvested only half of the trees it targeted for 1996 in Clayoquot Sound. Cutting is expected to come to a near halt this year.

Findlay said MacMillan is intent on improving the bottom lines of its core businesses. It has taken some steps already, including setting up its paper business as a stand-alone entity and selling its shipping unit for C$108 million ($80 million) in a deal to close in March.

But analysts have said those moves may not be enough to appease shareholders. "Clearly there will be additional pressure put on management over the next six months," a Toronto analyst said recently. "People are expecting more restructuring."
Some analysts have suggested MacMillan would have to cut its C60 cents (44 cents) a year dividend or raise up to C$400 million ($295 million) in debt in 1997.
